subject: english-literature
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: In tragedy, 'hubris' refers to:
options: excessive pride or overreaching that affronts the moral or divine order
the hero's humility before the gods
questions.explain: Hubris is overweening pride or presumption that violates limits and invites the hero's downfall.

questions.q: How is Othello characterised at the play's opening before Iago's poison takes hold?
options: As a dignified, eloquent and respected military commander
questions.explain: Othello first appears as a noble, self-possessed general whose composure Iago gradually destroys.

questions.q: In Tess of the d'Urbervilles, the protagonist's destruction by social judgement, chance and inflexible circumstance most closely fits the model of:
options: modern/social tragedy in which an essentially blameless figure is crushed by hostile forces
comic tragedy with a restorative ending
classical tragedy with a formal chorus
questions.explain: Tess exemplifies a modern tragedy of victimhood, undone by social cruelty and circumstance more than personal fault.

questions.q: What does Othello demand of Iago, in a line revealing his shift toward needing evidence?
options: 'I'll have some proof... the ocular proof'
questions.explain: Othello's demand for 'ocular proof' shows his fatal need for visible certainty Iago exploits.

questions.q: What is notable about Cassio's attitude toward Desdemona?
options: He is courteous and respectful, which Iago twists into evidence
He secretly loves her and plots with her
questions.explain: Cassio's genuine courtesy toward Desdemona is manipulated by Iago to suggest an affair.

questions.q: Shakespearean tragedy typically departs from strict classical models by:
options: mingling subplots, comic elements and a broad sweep of time and place
questions.explain: Shakespeare loosens the classical unities, weaving subplots, comedy and expansive action into the tragic structure.

questions.q: 'Nemesis' in the tragic pattern refers to:
options: the agent or process of retribution that brings the hero's downfall
the comic foil to the protagonist
questions.explain: Nemesis is the retributive force or fate that punishes the hero's transgression, completing the tragic arc.

questions.q: The convention of the 'tragic waste' refers to:
options: the destruction of much that is valuable, leaving a sense of loss beyond the hero alone
questions.explain: Tragic waste names the loss of admirable lives and potential, deepening the catastrophe's emotional weight.

questions.q: How does Iago manipulate Cassio into losing his position?
options: By getting Cassio drunk so he brawls and is dismissed
By forging a letter of treason
questions.explain: Iago plies Cassio with drink, provoking a fight that leads Othello to strip Cassio of his rank.

questions.q: The 'inciting incident' in a tragedy is best described as:
options: the event that sets the tragic chain of cause and effect in motion
questions.explain: The inciting incident triggers the causal sequence that drives the tragic action toward its catastrophe.

questions.q: Tragedy generally evokes a sense of 'inevitability' because:
options: cause and effect, character and fate combine so that the catastrophe feels both shocking and unavoidable
the plot is chosen at random
questions.explain: Tragic inevitability arises from the tight causal logic linking character, choice and fate toward the catastrophe.

questions.q: Which theme is most central to Othello?
options: Sexual jealousy and its destructive power
questions.explain: Jealousy, the 'green-eyed monster', drives Othello to destroy what he loves.

questions.q: In Aristotle's Poetics, 'hamartia' is best understood as:
options: the reversal of fortune from good to bad
the tragic hero's error of judgement or flaw that precipitates their downfall
the audience's emotional purging at the play's close
questions.explain: Hamartia is the tragic hero's mistake or flaw, the error from which the catastrophe ultimately flows.

questions.q: Othello was probably first performed around which period?
questions.explain: Othello dates to roughly 1603-04, early in the reign of James I.

questions.q: In tragedy, a 'foil' character functions to:
options: contrast with the hero so as to highlight the hero's qualities and choices
questions.explain: A foil sets off the protagonist by contrast, clarifying the hero's traits and the meaning of their decisions.

questions.q: How does Desdemona die at the end of the play?
options: Othello smothers her in their bed
questions.explain: Othello smothers Desdemona in her bed, convinced of her adultery.

questions.q: How does Othello describe himself in his final speech?
options: 'One that loved not wisely, but too well'
'A man more sinned against than sinning'
questions.explain: Othello asks to be remembered as one who 'loved not wisely, but too well' before killing himself.

questions.q: Why does the action move from Venice to Cyprus in Act 2?
options: Iago is posted there as governor
To pursue the Turkish fleet threatening Cyprus
questions.explain: Othello is sent to defend Cyprus against the Turks, though a storm destroys the Turkish fleet.

questions.q: How does Othello die?
options: He is executed by the Venetian state
He takes his own life with a hidden weapon
questions.explain: Othello stabs himself after recognising his terrible error, dying beside Desdemona.

questions.q: The Aristotelian 'tragic hero' is conventionally a figure who is:
options: of high estate and essentially noble, whose downfall arises from error rather than mere vice
wholly villainous and deserving of punishment
questions.explain: The classical tragic hero is elevated and largely virtuous, falling through hamartia rather than outright wickedness.

questions.q: The function of the 'chorus' in Greek tragedy was most often to:
options: stage the violent deeds on stage
comment on the action, voice communal response and offer moral or thematic reflection
play the role of the tragic hero
questions.explain: The chorus mediates between stage and audience, commenting on events and articulating the wider moral perspective.

questions.q: The 'tragic arc' of a conventional tragedy moves broadly:
options: from a position of stature, through error and reversal, to catastrophe and often recognition
in a circle returning to the start unchanged
questions.explain: The tragic arc descends from elevation through hamartia and peripeteia to catastrophe, often by way of anagnorisis.

questions.q: A 'modern tragedy' such as those theorised by Arthur Miller argues that the common man can be a tragic hero because:
options: tragic stature comes from the intensity of the struggle to secure one's dignity, not from high rank
questions.explain: Miller relocates tragic dignity in the ordinary individual's struggle for selfhood, breaking from the requirement of noble rank.

questions.q: What happens to Emilia in the final scene?
options: She takes her own life beside Desdemona
Iago kills her after she exposes his lies
questions.explain: Emilia reveals the truth about the handkerchief and Iago stabs her to silence her.

questions.q: How does the play treat the theme of race?
options: Race is praised as irrelevant by all characters
Othello is mocked only for his age
Othello as 'the Moor' is othered, and racist slurs mark his outsider status
questions.explain: Othello is repeatedly racialised as 'the Moor', and Iago and Brabantio deploy racist language to isolate him.

questions.q: The repeated contrast between Iago's reputation as 'honest' and his true nature illustrates which theme?
questions.explain: Iago is constantly called 'honest' even as he deceives, dramatising appearance versus reality.

questions.q: In Doctor Faustus, the overreaching protagonist who barters his soul for forbidden knowledge illustrates the tragic convention of:
options: aspiration and transgression punished by an inexorable downfall
the restoration of order through marriage
questions.explain: Faustus embodies tragic overreaching, his transgressive ambition driving an inescapable damnation.

questions.q: 'Catharsis' is frequently debated by critics because:
options: Aristotle defined it at exhaustive length
it appears only in modern drama
Aristotle left the term under-explained, prompting rival readings as purgation, purification or clarification
it refers solely to the hero's death
questions.explain: The brevity of Aristotle's account has generated competing interpretations of what catharsis actually achieves.

questions.q: How does Othello come to marry Desdemona?
options: By winning her in a contest set by the Duke
Through a betrothal organised by Iago
Through an arranged marriage by her father Brabantio
By eloping secretly, which Brabantio condemns to the Senate
questions.explain: Othello and Desdemona marry secretly, and Brabantio accuses Othello of bewitching her before the Senate.

questions.q: What role does Roderigo play in Iago's schemes?
options: He is Iago's trusting dupe, funding the plot to win Desdemona
questions.explain: Roderigo, in love with Desdemona, is exploited and bankrolled by Iago, who finally kills him.
